recipe.history:
Long before the fast-food era flattened the American burger into a gray, uniform disk, the all-beef patty was a point of pride — a declaration. The cultural lineage of the 100% beef burger traces back to the late 19th century, when German immigrants brought the concept of the Hamburg steak to American shores: coarsely ground beef, loosely packed, seared hard on a cast-iron griddle. What made it distinctly American was the democratic audacity of putting it between bread and handing it to a working person at a county fair or a lunch counter. The emphasis on purity — beef and only beef, nothing extended with fillers, binders, or mystery — emerged as a mark of quality in an era when adulteration of food was rampant and trust between diner and cook was hard-won. To say your burger was 100% beef was to make a promise.

Through the 20th century, the all-beef patty became the backbone of American burger culture in a way that transcended mere ingredient preference. Diners and drive-ins built their reputations on the quality of their beef blends — the ratio of chuck to brisket to short rib, the fat content, the grind size. Serious burger joints refused to press the patty down on the griddle, knowing that the juice running onto the flat-top was the very soul of the thing being sacrificed for nothing. The rise of regional styles — the smash burger of the Midwest, the thick pub-style patty of the Northeast, the open-flame char of the backyard South — all orbited the same gravitational center: quality beef, honestly prepared. The joke embedded in "Something's NOT Fishy" is the joke of a cook who refuses to cut corners, who meets suspicion with confidence, who lets the beef speak for itself.

I remember the first time a burger made me stop talking. I was maybe nine years old, sitting at a formica counter at a place my father loved, a no-name diner that smelled of rendered fat and coffee that had been on the burner since morning. The patty came out on a toasted bun with nothing but onion and mustard, and the first bite released a rush of beef fat and char that hit somewhere behind the eyes. There was no fish, no filler, no apology. It was just beef doing what beef does when someone respects it enough to leave it alone. That memory lives in the hands now — in how I pack a patty loosely, in how I wait for the crust to form before I even think about flipping, in the particular patience required to serve something that is exactly what it says it is.

Cooking a beef patty to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135°F — is not a preference. It is a philosophy, and like all good philosophies, it is grounded in physical reality. At medium rare, the muscle fibers have contracted just enough to firm the patty into something you can bite through cleanly, but the intramuscular fat has begun to render and distribute, coating every fiber in a slick of warm, beefy richness that well-done beef simply cannot offer. The Maillard reaction has done its work on the exterior, building a dark, savory crust of caramelized proteins and sugars that contrasts with the yielding, pink interior. To cook beyond this point is to drive off the moisture, tighten the fibers into something closer to leather, and erase the very qualities that make quality beef worth buying. A burger cooked to well-done is not a safe burger — it is a wasted one. Medium rare is the only honest answer to the question of what beef wants to be.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
600g freshly ground beef blend — 50% chuck (80/20), 25% brisket, 25% short rib
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed) for the griddle
Salt and white pepper to taste
4 leaves green leaf lettuce, washed and dried
1 large ripe beefsteak tomato, sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 medium yellow onion, sliced into thin rings
2 large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE DOUGH: Combine bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook. Add the warm milk and 2 eggs. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.
2. DEVELOP THE DOUGH: Increase mixer speed to medium and knead for 5 minutes until the dough becomes smooth and begins to pull away from the sides of the bowl.

3. ADD BUTTER: With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to be fully incorporated before adding the next. This process should take 8–10 minutes. The finished dough will be glossy, smooth, and slightly tacky.

4. FIRST RISE: Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or overnight. Cold fermentation develops flavor and makes the dough easier to shape.

5. SHAPE THE BUNS: Remove dough from the refrigerator and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Shape each portion into a tight ball by pulling the dough surface taut and pinching the seam at the bottom. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced at least 3 inches apart.
6. SECOND RISE: Cover loosely with plastic wrap and allow to proof at room temperature for 2–2.5 hours, until the buns have nearly doubled in size and look pillowy.

7. BAKE THE BUNS: Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp of water and gently brush the tops of the buns. Sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

8. MAKE THE SPECIAL SAUCE: Whisk together mayonnaise, sweet pickle relish, yellow mustard, ketchup, white wine vinegar, smoked paprika, garlic powder, and onion powder in a small bowl until fully combined. Season with salt and white pepper. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld.

9. CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: Melt butter with olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed skillet over medium-low heat. Add sliced onions, sugar, and salt. Stir to coat. Cook low and slow, stirring every 5–7 minutes, for 45–55 minutes until onions are deeply golden, jammy, and reduced. Add balsamic vinegar in the final 5 minutes and stir to incorporate. Set aside.

10. PREPARE THE BEEF: Remove your ground beef blend from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Gently divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 150g each). Do not overwork the meat — loosely shape each portion into a disk about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season generously on both sides with kosher salt and cracked black pepper just before cooking.
11. PREHEAT YOUR COOKING SURFACE: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat for at least 3 minutes until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil and swirl to coat.

12. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Place patties in the pan, working in batches if needed — do not crowd. Do not press down. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes until a dark, deeply caramelized crust has formed on the bottom. Flip once. Add a slice of cheese to each patty immediately after flipping. Cook for an additional 2–2.5 minutes. Pull patties when an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C). Transfer to a resting rack and tent loosely with foil for 2 minutes. The carry-over heat will bring the final temperature to a perfect medium rare.

13. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice the brioche buns in half. Place cut-side down on the hot griddle or a dry skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly toasted. Remove immediately.

14. BUILD THE BURGER: Spread a generous tablespoon of special sauce on the cut face of both the top and bottom buns. On the bottom bun, layer in this order: a leaf of green leaf lettuce, 1–2 slices of beefsteak tomato, the cheese-topped beef patty, a spoonful of caramelized onions, 4 bread-and-butter pickle chips, and a few rings of raw yellow onion for crunch and brightness.

15. CAP AND SERVE: Place the sauced top bun firmly over the assembled burger. Serve immediately while the patty is still resting at medium rare temperature, the bun is warm, and the cheese is molten. This burger is 100% beef. There is nothing fishy about it.
